# How to Build a Simple Weekly Schedule in Google Sheets with Gemini

> **In short:** You can ask Gemini, the AI built into Google Sheets, to design a weekly schedule from a plain description of your week — with time blocks, color categories, and a formula that totals hours automatically. You only need a Google account.

Most weeks you can list your time blocks in your head — work, gym, family dinner, the Saturday coffee — yet you never actually write them down. That's the gap this guide fills. In about ten minutes, you'll describe your week in plain English and end up with a color-coded schedule in Google Sheets that adds up your hours for you. The result is something you'll actually open on Sunday evening, not a spreadsheet that dies in your downloads folder.

## Before you start
- A Google account (free — the same one you use for Gmail).
- A computer or phone that can open Google Sheets: go to sheets.google.com in any browser, or install the free Google Sheets mobile app.
- Roughly 10 to 15 minutes, and a rough mental picture of what your week actually looks like.
- Some Gemini features inside Sheets are only available on paid Google plans — if you don't see the Gemini option, check Google's official pricing page for the latest plan details. A free workaround: draft the schedule at gemini.google.com first, then paste it into Sheets.

## Step 1 — Open Google Sheets and start fresh
Open sheets.google.com in your browser, or launch the Google Sheets app, and sign in with your Google account. Click the "+" button or "Blank spreadsheet" to create a new, empty sheet. Name it by clicking "Untitled spreadsheet" at the top-left and typing something you'll recognize later — "My weekly schedule" works fine.

💬 Example: name it "Spring weekly schedule" or "My week plan".

If it looks different: on a phone, the "+" usually sits in the bottom-right corner; if you only see templates, tap "Blank" inside that section. Menu wording changes often — just look for any option that creates a fresh, empty sheet.

You'll know it worked when you see a grid of empty cells with column letters (A, B, C…) across the top and row numbers (1, 2, 3…) down the side.

## Step 2 — Open the Gemini side panel
Look at the top-right corner of the Sheets window for a small sparkle ✨ icon or a button labeled something like "Help me" or "Ask Gemini." Click it. A side panel slides in from the right edge — this is your chat window, and you'll stay inside your spreadsheet the whole time.

💬 Example: type "Hi" as a quick first message to confirm Gemini is responding.

If it looks different: Gemini's exact location in Sheets has moved over the years. If you don't see a sparkle, open the "Tools" menu (sometimes labeled "Extensions" on older versions) and look for anything mentioning Gemini or "Ask." On Workspace accounts, your admin may need to turn Gemini on — if the option is entirely missing, ask your IT admin or check Google's help pages.

You'll know it worked when you can type a question into the side panel and an answer appears in the same panel within a few seconds.

## Step 3 — Describe your week and ask for a template
In the Gemini side panel, write a short paragraph describing a typical week. Be specific — even if it feels messy. Then ask for a weekly schedule layout with time blocks, categories you can color-code, and a formula that totals hours per category. Gemini will reply either with a written layout you can copy, or with a button to insert a table directly into your sheet.

💬 Example: "Here's my week. I work Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. I teach a yoga class Tuesday and Thursday evenings from 6 to 7:30 p.m. I hit the gym three mornings a week, around 6:30 to 7:30 a.m. on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. Saturday morning is family breakfast from 9 to 11 a.m. Please build a weekly schedule in this sheet with rows for each day, columns for morning, midday, afternoon, and evening, and a SUM formula that totals the hours automatically."

If it looks different: some versions of Gemini in Sheets can only chat (no insert button). If that happens, copy the layout into the cells yourself — see Step 4.

You'll know it worked when you see either a table inserted into the sheet or a clear text description of where each activity should go.

## Step 4 — Build the time-block grid yourself (the easy way)
If Gemini gave you a written description, copy it into your sheet by hand. In row 1, type the days of the week across the columns (Monday in A1, Tuesday in B1, and so on — or use one column per time slot if you prefer). In column A, starting from row 2, type your time blocks: "6:30–7:30 a.m.", "9:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m.", "6:00–7:30 p.m.", and so on. Then drop each activity into the cell where day and time meet.

💬 Example: in cell B2 (Tuesday morning) type "Gym"; in cell C5 (Wednesday afternoon) type "Deep work block"; in cell A8 (Monday evening) type "Family dinner."

If it looks different: some people prefer one row per day and one column per time slot — both are normal layouts. Choose the one that's easier to read on your device.

You'll know it worked when you can read down a column to see one full day's plan, or across a row to see one time slot across the week, without guessing.

## Step 5 — Add color categories so your eyes can scan it fast
Highlight the column or row headers by clicking the letter at the top of the column (or the row number on the left), then pick a fill color from the toolbar. Look for a paint-can icon or a "Fill color" button. Then color each activity by type: one color for work, one for fitness, one for family, one for rest. Pick colors that mean something to you.

💬 Example: blue for work, green for fitness, yellow for family time, gray for rest or sleep.

If it looks different: the fill-color icon sometimes looks like a tipped-over paint bucket. On a phone, the same tool lives inside the formatting menu, often marked with an "A" and color bars underneath it.

You'll know it worked when you can glance at the sheet and instantly see which parts of your week are work, which are fitness, and which are family time — without reading a single word.

## Step 6 — Add a formula that totals your hours
At the bottom of one day's column, click an empty cell and type a SUM formula. In Sheets, every formula starts with `=`. If you've put the duration of each activity in plain numbers (8 for an 8-hour workday, 1.5 for a 90-minute class), the formula adds them up for you.

💬 Example: type `=SUM(B2:B10)` and press Enter. The cell instantly shows the total. If your durations are in seconds, multiply by 24 first: `=SUM(B2:B10)*24`.

If it looks different: if your time blocks are written as text like "9–5", Sheets can't add them up — they'd need to be plain numbers in a separate "Hours" column. Ask Gemini in the side panel, "How do I add up time blocks written as text in Sheets?" if you get stuck.

You'll know it worked when the total cell shows a number that updates the moment you edit any of the time blocks above it — that's the formula doing its job.

## Step 7 — Save once and forget about it
Look at the top-left of the screen for your file name. As long as you're signed in, Google Sheets saves your work automatically every few seconds — there's no "Save" button to click. If you see a small gray "Saving…" message or a checkmark next to the title, you're done.

💬 Example: just close the browser tab when you finish. Next time you open the file, your schedule will be right where you left it.

You'll know it worked when you can refresh the page or close and reopen the file and find your schedule exactly as it was.

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake: asking Gemini something too vague.** "Make me a schedule" gives a generic template that won't fit your life. **Always include your real hours, real activities, and how many days — the more specific you are, the better the output.**
- **Mistake: writing time blocks as text like "9–5".** Sheets can't add text up, so your total stays at zero. **Fix: put the duration as a plain number in a separate "Hours" column (8 for an 8-hour workday, 1.5 for a 90-minute class), or ask Gemini how to convert time strings to numbers.**
- **Mistake: assuming Gemini inserted your schedule when it only chatted.** Some versions of Gemini in Sheets can only suggest, not insert. **Fix: read the side panel carefully — if you see an "Insert" button, click it; otherwise copy the suggestions into the cells yourself.**

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A weekly schedule you actually open turns vague plans into real commitments. The color categories mean you can spot at a glance if "rest" has quietly disappeared from your week — and fix it before burnout shows up.
- **For your business or work:** If you bill by the hour or track project time, the SUM formula and color categories double as a rough time-tracking sheet. Swap the activity names for your projects and you have a one-page weekly dashboard.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't aim for the perfect schedule in one sitting. Type in the bones of your week today — work, sleep, family — and add the rest over a few days as you notice the gaps.

## Try it now
Open a new Google Sheet, open the Gemini side panel, and paste this in: "I teach three morning classes Monday, Wednesday, and Friday from 8 to 11 a.m. I work part-time Tuesday and Thursday from 1 to 6 p.m. I have family dinner every weekday at 7 p.m. Build me a weekly schedule with time blocks, three color categories (teaching, work, family), and a SUM formula that totals hours per category." See what it gives you, change the colors to match your real life, and you've got a planner that took ten minutes to make and will save you hours of "wait, what day is it again?" by next Sunday.
